uncited: The family shares a core mechanism: for each pixel, a ray is constructed from the camera through the pixel center into the volume domain.

The transformation is $\hat{B}_{\beta_1, \beta_2, \beta_3} = T^{-1}_{\beta_1}^{\alpha_1} T^{-1}_{\beta_2}^{\alpha_2} T^{-1}_{\beta_3}^{\alpha_3} B_{\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \alpha_3}$, where $T$ is the bounding tetrahedron matrix.
It uses FBM of Perlin noise (2nd order Lipschitz) with improved quadratic bounds and enhancements for basic scenes.
For non-2nd-order-Lipschitz noise, it uses only enhancements applicable to linear bounds.
For Hypertextures, it uses FBM field of Perlin noise with quadratic bounds and varying SDF thresholds, leveraging BVH and Early Stop to avoid manual bounding spheres.
Intersects scan planes (the z extension of scan lines) with each volume element to form intersection polygons.
These intersection polygons are broken into spans.
The pixels of each span are integrated front-to-back to generate opacity.
For collided pixels, the ray direction is negated in Z ($ray\_d\_sc = (ray\_d.x, ray\_d.y, -ray\_d.z)$).
The dot product with the normal is computed, and a reflection vector $r$ is derived.
It trilinearly interpolates data values at the ray-voxel entry and exit points.
Target values are classified into three categories: (1) strictly between entry and exit values, (2) not between but one endpoint is within its allowable window, or (3) neither.
For Category 1, the relative distance $t$ is parameterized using linear interpolation.
Shows isosurfaces by mapping the corresponding data values to almost opaque values and the rest to transparent values.
The concept of rendering isosurfaces from volumetric data dates back to the early 1990s.
